1. Sarah tidies the balcony and sets Emma's rabbit, the one Emma sleeps with, out on the railing to air, so a Steinmarder takes it from the rail and carries it in through the roof vent; Noah sees the tail go through the vent and shouts where it went, and Sarah says aloud that the Estrich has one small window, that its light is gone by six, and that whoever wants the rabbit must go up now; Emma wants the rabbit more than anything, but she is afraid of the dark, so she stays at the foot of the ladder with the scarf Hans knitted her pulled tight, which is what she does whenever she is frightened, and she pushes her small torch into Noah's hand instead of climbing.

2. Daniel says the big torch is dead because he forgot the batteries again, and he goes out to look for some, so Emma's torch is the only light and it goes up with Noah; Noah blocks the marten with a broom instead of hitting it, but the marten backs behind the water tank and both the rabbit and the torch drop into the narrow gap beside it, and when Noah pushes his hand in, his fingers stop at the knuckles; he comes down with a scraped wrist, angry and ashamed, and he says that only Emma's hand is small enough.

3. Hans holds the ladder and tries once to keep Emma off it because he is frightened for her, and he will not carry his candle lantern up, since he has allowed no open flame under a roof since he was a boy; Emma is afraid, but she lets go of his hand and climbs anyway, asking him to hum so she knows where the bottom is, and as she reaches the top the light in the roof window goes out; in the dark her hand fits the gap, she feels her rabbit's wool held under the marten's paws, and beside it she feels four small young in a nest of moss and thread, so she understands that the marten will not let go of anything soft.

4. Emma pulls the scarf off her neck and lays it into the gap in front of the marten, and the same paws let go of the small rabbit to seize the bigger wool and drag it to the young under the tiles, which is where Emma names it Ruess and says they will leave it alone; she climbs down the dark ladder herself, one rung at a time, with Hans humming and then coming two rungs up to meet her; at the bottom she stands with a bare neck, holding the rabbit, telling Hans what the dark looks like from the inside, and she is proud.

# CLOTHING REQUIREMENTS

Never a vest or singlet, a bare chest or midriff, or a one-piece or nightdress.
- **A character the story already dresses for their role stays `standard`** — a working captain, a uniformed officer, a baker at their own oven. Their own outfit IS their clothing in this world, and the theme's costume puts a second set of clothes on someone who came dressed. Costume the characters the theme is a costume FOR.
- **A garment the story turns on is described IN FULL in the outfit that wears it** — a garment the arc or plan has someone hold, lend, wrap or lose goes in the outfit of the character who wears it first (the one the plan first gives it to, when no one wears it), as the garment they name, with colour, material and what makes this one recognisable, in the slot it occupies. The Visual Bible copies those words for its own entry of the same object, so the two never describe it differently. - An outfit `description` is appearance only: garments, colours, materials, fastenings. No page numbers, no events, no other character or creature, no carried item or what a pocket holds. A garment a page takes off stays in the outfit as worn; the `wornItems` row of that page records it off, never the outfit.
- `garments` lists every garment `description` names, one row each: `slot` is where on the body it is worn, exactly one of `headwear`, `top`, `bottom`, `footwear`, `belt/waist`, `outer layer`, `accessories`; `name` is the garment's noun phrase as `description` words it, without its colour ("hooded anorak", "canvas trainers"); `colour` is its main colour, one of red, blue, green, yellow, orange, purple, brown, black, white, grey and nothing else, or omitted when the garment has no single main colour. - A garment belongs to ONE outfit: that of the character who wears it first. When the plan hands it to another character — to hold, wrap, wear or keep — the plan line and that page's `wornItems` row carry the handoff; the receiver's outfit never names it. No two outfits name the same garment.
- **A prop is not a garment.** A garment is clothing a person wears: coat, scarf, hat, cloak, boots. A blanket, towel, sheet, tablecloth, bag, umbrella, toy, tool or any other object that is carried, held, spread out, shared or wrapped around someone for a page is a story prop, never a garment: no outfit names it, however the plan uses it. The plan line and the Visual Bible carry a prop.

Dungarees, pinafore, suspenders, kilt, kimono, sari and similar render as plain garments when only named: keep the garment name in front and spell out its parts ("denim dungaree shorts — square bib panel over the chest held by two shoulder straps").
